newsitem.title: NORWAY: STOREBRAND SHARE JUMPS ON 1996 PROFITS.
newsitem.headline: STOREBRAND SHARE JUMPS ON 1996 PROFITS.

text.p: Storebrand ASA, Norway's biggest insurance company, said on Wednesday weaker non-life results burdened 1996 group profits, but the result still beat market expectations and the share price soared.

Storebrand said 1996 group profits fell 13.6 percent to 1.25 billion crowns ($179.7 million) but financial portfolio gains helped offset some of the losses and a restructuring programme was beginning to have an effect.

Storebrand was up more than four percent at 47.50 crowns in brisk trade in the early afternoon on the Oslo Bourse because of the result and market talk that a major investor was seeking to take control of the company.
"The result surprised the market but the price is also up because of speculation on what is happening with Storebrand," one dealer said.
The Storebrand Group recorded an operating profit before distribution to the life assurance policyholders of 4.12 billion crowns, or 86 million less than in 1995.
After distributing to the customers their share of the profit from life and pension insurance, the group's profit was 1.25 billion crowns, compared to 1.45 billion in 1995.

The life assurance operation benefited from the thriving capital markets. The operating result was 3.43 billion crowns, up from 3.34 billion. Net gains on the sale of securities totalled 1.68 billion crowns, compared with 964 million in 1995.
For non-life insurance the operating profit was 1.04 billion crowns, down from 1.18 billion. The weaker result was blamed partly on more claims referring to damage by fire and water.
The earnings per share fell to 4.10 crowns from 4.94 in 1995. The board proposed a dividend of 0.70 crowns per preferential share, unchanged from 1995.
Storebrand President and Chief Executive Officer Age Korsvold said the insurer in 1996 had focused on implementing projects aimed at improving competitiveness.
"I think certainly that, being in the middle of a restructuring programme, our cost performance will improve in 1997," he told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV).
"In the final outcome, the financial results will determine whether we will maintain this level or whether we will be able to increase it somewhat in 1997," he said.
Earlier, he said gains of more than 200 million crowns had been realised at the end of 1996 as a result of a campaign to improve non-life insurance operations.

"These gains will be even higher this year and Storebrand maintains its objective of achieving annual gains of between 300 million and 500 million crowns in 1997 as a result of these improvement measures," Korsvold said.
Furthermore the company had started staff reductions expected to save 250 million crowns this year, he said.
Korsvold said he did not know who had been buying large amounts of shares in the company recently. Market players last week reported Storebrand shares were in demand.

News media have suggested that Norwegian entrepreneur and investor Kjell Inge Roekke, top shareholder in industrial group Aker RGI ASA, is the secret buyer of Storebrand stock and that he is seeking to take control.
Roekke was not available, but an Aker RGI spokesman said: "Aker RGI has not bought any shares in Storbrand."
